name: Erik Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run my own little guitar school from a rented room above a barber's on the high street, about twenty-five pupils a week, kids after school and adults in the evenings. Mornings I film short lessons and sell them as an online course, and I use AI for nearly everything behind the scenes: lesson plans, writing out tabs, the adverts. Weekends I play lead guitar in a covers band doing pubs and the odd festival.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Growing, but every penny goes back in. The room is three hundred a month, the website and software another sixty, and I bought a second amp in September. So I've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank, even though I'm busier than ever. My girlfriend Nadia works at a pharmacy and thinks I'm mad, but she also helps me with the accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people panicking wasted a lot of energy, and the people who just got on with it did fine. Online I'd post a video about how I use AI tools to run a one-man business. I'd probably get a few new pupils from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a plateau is good for me. The tools save me ten hours a week and nobody gets replaced. If AI stays a helper, I'm a one-man guitar school with a free assistant, and the only thing that can sink me is a bad winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow to thirty pupils by spring and think about hiring a second teacher one evening a week. I'd keep using the tools for marketing and lesson plans. And I'd finally start keeping a month's costs in a separate account, because Nadia's been asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, mostly. A bit uneasy about money, because I've built this on a thin floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a bad winter look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: January, when people cancel lessons after Christmas spending and the band has no bookings. Last January I made about half my usual month and paid the room rent on a credit card. I paid it off by March, but I didn't sleep well in February.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not keep more money aside instead of buying the second amp?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. I tend to bet on growth, and it's usually worked. But Nadia's right that one bad month could cost me the room, and without the room I've got no school.

I'd post a **video** on running a one-man business with AI.
think: A plateau is **good for me**, because AI saves ten hours a week.
Only a **bad winter** can really sink the school.
do: Consider hiring a **second teacher** one evening a week.
Keep **one month's costs** in a separate account.
feel: Mostly **good**, a bit **uneasy** about building on a thin floor.

He paid the room rent on a **credit card** last January.
He admits a habit of **betting on growth** over saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for small businesses that move fast, and I'd mean it. I'd tell other teachers to use the tools before their customers do. I wouldn't want new rules slowing everyone down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the online course sales drop, because an AI tutor can teach a beginner chords for nothing. Adults who'd come to me might try the app first. The online guitar course I filmed is about to compete with a free tutor that never gets tired, so the room above the barber's has to carry everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the online course and put everything into the room: group classes, a kids' rock band club on Saturdays, and gigs for pupils at the pub. I'd automate all the bookings, payments and reminders with AI. And I'd stop buying gear for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but excited. I like a challenge more than I like a quiet life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A kids' rock band club. Who's that for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten- to fifteen-year-olds who want to play in a band, not just practise alone in their bedroom. Parents would pay maybe twelve a session for a real band experience. No app gives a kid the feeling of playing loud with their mates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else in your line of work would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older guitar teacher in town, Malcolm, who still takes bookings by phone. He's sixty and won't touch a computer. I'd offer him a few evenings in my room, honestly, because his pupils trust him.

I don't want **new rules** slowing everyone down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stand on their own feet and look after their families, and the government should cut taxes and red tape so small firms can survive. I'd say it online and to the band. I'd also say this is when communities find out what they're made of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, two years and anything I do on a screen is gone, and adults who lose office jobs stop paying for guitar lessons. The teaching in the room is hands-on, so I'd have until about 2031, if parents can still pay. I built my whole guitar school on AI tools, and AGI by 2028 would turn those same tools into my competition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the school back to what pays: kids' groups and the band club. I'd move in with Nadia at her parents' place to save my share of rent, with a proper plan to move out. I'd also start fixing and selling second-hand guitars, which I already do a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and angry with myself for building on such a thin floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said about three years before the robots. What do you do with those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Squeeze every bit out of the hands-on stuff: kids' groups, the band, repairs. Put every spare penny into paying off the credit card and saving. And look at what lasts after 2031, maybe fixing and building instruments by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Nadia's job at the pharmacy: what happens to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The checking and the stock ordering could go to AI, she reckons, but someone still hands out the medicine and talks to the old folk. So I think she'd keep work, at least till the robots. Her job might end up carrying us both for a while, which would be humbling.

say: People need to stand on their **own feet** and look after family.
The government should cut **taxes and red tape** for small firms.

Adults who lose **office jobs** stop paying for lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone with a bit of get-up-and-go. Small businesses should move first and not wait for a government scheme. I'd share what I'm doing so other teachers can copy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years suits someone like me, if I start this year. The online stuff fades early, then adults drift off as office jobs go around 2031. Five years gives me time to turn a one-man guitar school into a place where kids come to play in bands and get their guitars fixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a guitar repair and setup course, about six hundred, and add repairs to the school by next year. I'd take on a pupil as a paid apprentice teacher for the beginner groups. I'd use AI to run all the admin and marketing, and save a hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but mostly fired up. I like a plan with a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An apprentice teacher. Can you afford that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only part-time, maybe eight hours a week, paid from the extra group classes. One of my older pupils, Jamal, is seventeen and brilliant with the little ones. I'd rather pay a local kid than a franchise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years change anything with Nadia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd get engaged sooner, probably next year. Her family's quite traditional, and so am I, and we'd want to marry before kids. Five years feels like enough to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone willing to work. Learn a trade, start something, look after your family. I'd say the government's job is mostly to stay out of the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'd be thirty-seven, with maybe a family. The online stuff still fades in the next few years, before AGI. Ten years is long enough to build a proper music shop with repairs and lessons, and short enough that I can't waste a single year of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the school steadily, add repairs in two years, and aim for a small shop with a teaching room by about 2030. I'd put money into the business only after keeping three months of costs aside. I'd use every AI tool going for the admin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly confident, a little anxious. The money's still thin, and that doesn't change because the deadline moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with the shop plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent going up on the high street, or me borrowing too much too soon. I've watched two shops on our street close in three years. I'd want to own the stock, not owe on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And in 2039, when the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then I'd hope the shop is a place people come to, not just a service. Kids playing in bands in the back room, old guys swapping stories by the amps. A robot can fix a guitar, maybe, but I doubt it can run a place like that.

The government's job is mostly to stay **out of the way**.

I can't waste a **single year** of the ten.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it turns the tools I built my business on into my competition, and I'd have no money to pivot. What would help is lower taxes and less red tape for small businesses, and cheap loans for people starting a trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what my pupils think. Kids who come to my guitar school don't want a perfect teacher; they want somebody who once failed the same chord and laughed about it.

headlineQuote: Kids who come to my guitar school don't want a perfect teacher; they want somebody who once failed the same chord and laughed about it.
portrait: Erik is a **27-year-old guitarist** who runs a one-man guitar school above a barber's.
He reinvests everything, leaving about **two weeks** of savings, to his girlfriend Nadia's worry.
He uses **AI daily** and sees fast change as a chance for small firms.
He wants **low taxes** and little red tape, and prefers hiring a local apprentice.
His plan grows from **kids' band clubs** to repairs and, with time, a small music shop.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his own AI tools would become his competition.
whatWouldHelp: **Lower taxes** and less red tape for small businesses.
**Cheap loans** for people starting a trade.
